text:
A suspension bridge carries load from the deck to the ground by turning a messy collection of downward forces into one large tension path. The traffic loads arrive at the deck as moving wheels, but even a single axle is too small to be the basic structural unit, so the roadway is built like a light, stiff platform. Edge beams, longitudinal girders, transverse diaphragms, and sometimes arched deck ribs collect those forces and spread them along the span. The deck still matters: it distributes load, resists local bending, keeps the roadway straight, and controls cross-sectional sway. But it is not the element that spans the main gap, because bending a long thin slab across a huge clear span would require an impossibly deep member. Suspension design solves that by letting cables, placed at the top, do most of the long-span work.

From ordinary deck positions, vertical suspenders drop from the main cable to the deck edge or to the deck structure. Each suspender carries essentially axial tension: the deck pushes down on it, and it pulls up on the cable. Along the span, the number and spacing of suspenders are set so that the load arriving from each panel of deck is carried upward without excessive local bending in the cable or stress concentration in the suspenders. The main cable is shaped to match the load. If its shape is parabolic and the load along the span were evenly distributed, the cable would carry only tension with little bending; in real bridges the load is not uniform, because traffic moves, deck mass varies, and temperature changes growth, so the cable is close to parabolic but not exactly. Tension increases toward the towers where the cable descends, and the cable’s curvature gives it an internal resultant that has both a vertical component and a horizontal component.

That horizontal component is the crucial part of the whole system. At each tower, the cable presses sideways outward as well as downward. Saddles or saddle seats pass the cable over the tower top and help align it, but the tower does not merely support the cable in a simple vertical shelf. It must absorb the combined action of the cables: they pull upward along their slopes and push outward toward the ends of the bridge. The tower legs respond mainly by compression, while also resisting bending and sidesway from traffic, wind, temperature, and earthquakes. The legs are tapered or shaped to control that response. A tall, slender tower would be too sensitive to sideways wind; a stiff, massive one wastes material and complicates anchorage. The bridge engineer therefore balances height, weight, stiffness, and cost.

At the ends, the cables are not left floating. They run downhill to anchorages at the abutments or to backstays connected to massive concrete blocks, rock, or soil. These details turn the outward thrust of the cables into something the ground can resist. The horizontal cable pull is resisted by the mass and friction of the anchorage, by the geometry between tower and anchorage, or by a system of stays that carry the tension into foundations. The vertical component of cable force is added to the load on the towers and abutments. At the foundations, the bridge’s total weight, the downward components of cable force, and the effects of uplift or overturning are transferred into the soil or rock. Foundations are sized so they can bear the downward pressure without excessive settlement, resist lateral sliding, and resist overturning from wind or large moving loads.

The ground is the final boundary condition, but it is also where the design is allowed to differ. A bridge over soft ground needs very large or deep foundations. A bridge on rock can carry larger forces with less mass. In both cases the structure is designed as a chain: roadway to girders and diaphragms to suspenders to cables to towers and anchorages to foundations to earth. That chain must remain continuous under dead load, live load, braking, wind, thermal expansion, construction eccentricity, and fatigue from repeated traffic. Creep and temperature change the cable shape and therefore the internal forces, so engineers include allowance for sag, movement, and stress. A suspension bridge is therefore not “held up” by the towers alone. The towers, cables, deck, and foundations form one connected system in which vertical load is collected, converted into tension, carried sideways into the towers and anchorages, and finally delivered to the ground with enough strength, stiffness, and durability to carry traffic safely for decades.
